extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teacher educators and middle-level teachers (participants and course designers for the M2 Institute/graduate program)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, delivering, and assessing graduate-level mathematics courses for middle-level teachers (course structure, problem selection, instructional style, portfolio/end-of-course assessment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits of Mind Problems: problem selection qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems need not be connected to the mathematics being studied but they should be solvable. Ideal problems involve experimentation or consideration of special cases and require careful reasoning and creativity to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems should encourage experimentation, special-case exploration, pattern-finding, and require creativity (example: Downtown Mathville path-counting). They may be concrete or abstract and are intended to develop mathematical habits of mind. Anti-pattern: trivial exercises tied only to recent syntax or rote practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active learning instructional style
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction emphasizes active learning: participants are given a problem to solve and work in groups, often discovering multiple solution approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class routines include group work, multiple instructors in the room (example: class size 32–35 with five instructors), staff advisors for small-group meetings, presentations by participants followed by mini-lectures, and study groups with instructional team support. Instructors intervene to help only when participants are 'stuck' to promote productive struggle ('Don't help me now, I need to figure this out on my own').

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and peer sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: After solutions are found, selected participants present solutions to the class, often showing different approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentations are followed by mini-lectures that explain the intended learning. Peer presentation is both a formative assessment opportunity and a mechanism to expose multiple solution strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework workload and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each night participants have three to four hours of homework; study groups and instructional team members assist as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework is substantial and intended to promote deep engagement. Graduate students provide written feedback on submitted homework; instructors may ask for rework or resubmission if work is unsatisfactory. Excessive direct help is avoided to maintain learning benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-Course Assignment: composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: End-of-course assignments are comprehensive take-home finals with three components: new mathematics problems covering course content, a 'super six' (or seven), and a reflection component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The End-of-Course assignment is the primary determiner of course grades. It reinforces polished final solutions and long-term retention. Written comments are offered on problems without providing a point total. Participants typically have four to six weeks to complete it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super six (polished solutions) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'super six' are polished solutions to problems that participants completed during the course which they are particularly proud of or which demonstrate their mathematical growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants include a short description of what the 'super' problems represent for their mathematical learning. This reinforces topics and encourages replacement of draft solutions by final polished solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative assessment emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment is more formative than summative; goal is to provide useful feedback to help teachers develop problem-solving ability and meet expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent formative feedback occurs via class presentations, small-group homework discussions, written comments from graduate students, and study-group interactions. Participants may be encouraged to revise solutions for their own benefit and for grade improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a rubric to assess teacher progress and commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: The course uses a rubric that assesses the teachers' achievements, their progress in the course, and their commitment to learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubric is used alongside written feedback and End-of-Course assignments to determine grades and to guide opportunities for reworking submissions to meet standards. (Rubric referenced as present; specific rubric items available on course website.)

rubrics_metrics.name: ECR portfolio components and grading weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment in Experimentation, Conjecture, and Reasoning (ECR) is based on a portfolio containing Solidifying Ideas, New Ideas, Habits of Mind solutions, Post-Tests, and Essays on Proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course grade weighting: homework from sub-sessions 50%, post-tests 25%, Teaching and Learning Activity 10%, End-of-Course Problem set 10%, responses/critiques on Blackboard 5%. Feedback allows redoing assignments; portfolio items receive comments to guide improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: ECR problem design criteria (AMC adaptations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are often adapted from AMC8/AMC10 items: non-standard, multi-step, combine facts/skills from multiple areas, and often require creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMC items are converted from multiple-choice to free-response by removing choices; items are selected to be accessible to middle-level teachers (e.g., no algebra on AMC8) and to counter the notion of mathematics as a strict topic sequence. Problems should provoke experimentation, conjecture, and reasoning rather than rote application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology as part of problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology (GeoGebra, MapleTA, Blackboard, Adobe Connect) is central to instruction and assessment, especially for geometry and online components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants use GeoGebra for geometric constructions and numeric exploration before symbolic solution; MapleTA administers and scores pre/post-tests; Blackboard supports documents and discussion; Adobe Connect for teleconferencing. Technology use includes measurement, experimentation, and construction of conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and Teaching Project (LTP) components and evaluative focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The LTP asks participants to design a lesson for their students and report on transferring challenging curriculum topics into their classroom; main components include a solution of the mathematics problem, an explanation of how the teacher adapted and taught the problem, copies of student work, a videotape of the lesson, and a written reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written reflection must include how students did on the problem, how they were assessed, and unexpected results. The course website includes the rubric used to assess LTP materials; evaluation focuses on quality of transfer to K–12 classroom, assessment of student learning, and reflective analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of multiple representations and curricular connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction and tasks should draw connections among arithmetic, algebraic, and geometric representations and employ concrete examples and representations relevant to middle level curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because participants use many curricula, course connections are not tied to a single program. Representations (family trees, manipulatives, charts, diagrams, algebraic generalizations) are emphasized. Example: modular arithmetic introduced via days-of-week boxes to build intuition for congruence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations for participant solutions: reasoning, generalization, and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants are expected to progress from example-based responses to explanations that generalize patterns, provide algebraic representations when possible, and clearly communicate mathematical reasoning in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors value solutions that move beyond assertion to pattern identification, generalization, and justification (e.g., moving from enumerating Pythagorean triples to noting patterns and searching for general formulas). Growth is measured by increased use of text to explain thinking and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: NT&C assessment types and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Number Theory & Cryptology (NT&C) assessment includes daily homework completion grades, participation in problem sessions and presentations, and an End-of-Course problem set; participants are encouraged to work in groups but submit their own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed problems vary from computational tasks to straightforward proofs and proofs requiring significant insight. Feedback focuses on strengthening mathematical reasoning and written communication. Course selection of proofs emphasizes accessibility and relevance to middle-level teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity and mechanism for revision and grade improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When participants are disappointed by a grade, the program offers the opportunity to rework solutions to meet standards and merit a higher grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice this can involve resubmission of assignments, private meetings with instructors, or targeted rework of End-of-Course materials; instructors provide written comments without point totals to guide revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem accessibility and scaffolding for teachers lacking proof fluency
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs and theoretical material are selected or presented at a level accessible to middle-level teachers: give key ideas, examples, or evidence rather than full rigorous proofs when unnecessary for classroom teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers are given experiences proving easy statements (e.g., parity lemmas) to build proof fluency before encountering more complex theorems (e.g., Unique Factorization, Fermat’s Little Theorem) which are presented with key ideas or motivating examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio evidence of transfer to K–12 student learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of K–12 students' work in a teacher’s LTP correlates with the quality/depth of the teacher’s own solution and generalization abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider not only the teacher’s mathematical solution but also how well that understanding was transferred to students (student work samples, videotape, assessment results, and reflective analysis).
